'''Michael A. Mares''' is an American [[zoologist]], academic, and author. He is the Emeritus Director and Curator at the [[Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History|Sam Noble Museum]], as well as a [[Professor Emeritus]] in the Department of Biology at the [[University of Oklahoma]].<ref name=yy>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ou.edu/cas/biology/people/faculty/michael-mares.html|title=Michael A. Mares|first=Biology Social|last=Media|website=www.ou.edu|access-date=2023-08-16|archive-date=2018-04-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180403131450/http://www.ou.edu/cas/biology/people/faculty/michael-mares.html}}</ref>

Mares is the recipient of the 2008 Jackson Award for exceptional service to the [[American Society of Mammalogists]]<ref name=A>{{Cite web|url=https://www.normantranscript.com/news/local_news/new-ou-welcomes-mares-back-to-museum-director-job/article_7d4fbc1c-6deb-5831-85f4-e6c117940c5b.html|title=OU welcomes Mares back to museum director job|date=August 1, 2008|website=Norman Transcript}}</ref> and is most known for his works on [[convergent evolution]], conservation, [[biogeography]], [[systematics]], and ecology of small [[mammals]]. He is the co-editor of ''Latin American Mammalogy: History, Biodiversity, and Conservation''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://squ.on.worldcat.org/search?queryString=bn:9780806123431|title=Latin American mammalogy: history, biodiversity, and conservation – Sultan Qaboos University}}</ref> and the author of ''A Desert Calling: Life in a Forbidding Landscape''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://squ.on.worldcat.org/search?queryString=bn:9780674040588|title=A desert calling: life in a forbidding landscape – Sultan Qaboos University}}</ref>

==Education==
Mares completed his Bachelor of Science in Biology from the [[University of New Mexico]]. Later, he obtained a Master of Science in Biology from [[Fort Hays Kansas State University]] and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in Zoology from the [[University of Texas]].<ref name=yy/>

==Career==
In 1972, Mares joined the [[Universidad Nacional de Tucumán]] as an adjunct professor of Zoology and later became a visiting professor of Ecology in 1974. From 1973 to 1981, he was an Assistant/[[Associate Professor]] of [[Biological Sciences]] at the [[University of Pittsburgh]]. In 1981, he joined the University of Oklahoma, where he held multiple appointments including serving as Professor of Zoology and Curator of Mammals at the [[Stovall Museum]] from 1983 to 2018. Over the years, he has held appointments as Joseph Brandt Professor from 1983 to 2003, Affiliate Faculty Member at the School of International and Area Studies from 2000 to 2018 and Presidential Professor from 2008 to 2018. In addition, he has been a Research Associate at the Museum of [[Texas Tech University]] since 2001 and the Museum of Southwestern Biology since 2011. Since 2018, he has been a Curator and Director Emeritus at the Sam Noble Museum and holds the title of Professor Emeritus in the Department of Biology.<ref name=yy/>

Mares was the President of the American Society of Mammalogists from 2010 to 2012, and the President of the Natural Science Collections Alliance from 2007 to 2009. Since 1983–2003 and 2008–2018, he served as the Director of Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History; he was a Fulbright Scholar to Argentina in 1986 and served on the Fulbright Board of Directors in the 1980s–1990s.<ref name=yy/>

==Research==
Mares' zoology research has won him the 1989 Don W. Tinkle Research Excellence Award from the Southwestern Association of Naturalists.<ref name=B>{{Cite web|url=http://vmpincel.ou.edu/swan/disaeng.htm|title=Southwestern Association of Naturalists|website=vmpincel.ou.edu}}</ref> He also won the 2000 [[C. Hart Merriam Award]] from the American Society of Mammalogists. He has authored more than 200 publications spanning the areas of species diversity, invasive species, and wildlife ecology including books and articles in peer-reviewed journals.<ref name=EXT>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/10/24/science/extinction-turns-be-slow-slow-process-some-severely-depleted-species-adapt.html|title=Extinction Turns Out to Be a Slow, Slow Process; Some Severely Depleted Species Adapt to Altered Habitats and Hang On for Years, Puzzling Biologists|work=The New York Times |date=24 October 2000 |last1=Revkin |first1=Andrew C. }}</ref>

===Conservation===
Mares' conservation research has explored the behavior of animal species in their natural habitats.<ref>{{cite book|first=M.A.|last=Mares|date=1982|chapter=Conservation of South American mammals|title=In Mammalian Biology in South America|editor-first1= M. A.|editor-last1= Mares |editor-first2= H. H.|editor-last2= Genoways}}</ref> Focusing his research efforts on conservation of South American mammals with Argentina as a paradigm,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/256416674|title=Conservation of South American Mammals: Argentina as a paradigm}}</ref> his work offered insights into the legal exportation of wildlife from Argentina<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Faunal Commercialization and Conservation in South America|author1=Mares, Michael A.|author2=Ojeda, Ricardo A.|year=1984|journal=BioScience|volume=34|issue=9|pages=580–584|doi=10.2307/1309601|jstor=1309601 }}</ref> and provided solutions related to conservation in South America.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Conservation in South america: problems, consequences, and solutions|first=M. A.|last=Mares|date=August 15, 1986|journal=Science|volume=233|issue=4765|pages=734–739|doi=10.1126/science.233.4765.734|pmid=17835182|bibcode=1986Sci...233..734M |s2cid=29681312 }}</ref> Furthermore, his book ''Latin American Mammalogy: History, Biodiversity, and Conservation'' addressed the preservation strategy and management concerning the significant transformations occurring in the natural landscapes of Latin America.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://squ.on.worldcat.org/search?queryString=bn:9780806123431|title=Latin American mammalogy: history, biodiversity, and conservation – WorldCat}}</ref> Moreover, he examined the contributions made by collections and museums to conservation biology and underscored the significance of integrating these institutions and their associated research efforts to develop a comprehensive program for conservation education.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/256114638|title=Natural history museums: working toward the development of a conservation ethic.}}</ref><ref name=EXT/>

===Evolution===
Mares' research on convergent evolution has studied the interactions between evolutionary processes and ecological dynamics.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=South American mammal zoogeography: evidence from convergent evolution in desert rodents.|first=M A|last=Mares|date=May 16, 1975|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=72|issue=5|pages=1702–1706|doi=10.1073/pnas.72.5.1702|pmid=1057165|pmc=432613 |bibcode=1975PNAS...72.1702M |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title=Convergent Evolution of Desert Rodents: Multivariate Analysis and Zoogeographic Implications|author=Mares, Michael A.|year=1976|journal=Paleobiology|volume=2|issue=1|pages=39–63|doi=10.1017/S0094837300003298 |jstor=2400196 |bibcode=1976Pbio....2...39M |s2cid=89417689 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/256095793|title=Convergent Evolution Among Desert Rodents: A Global Perspective}}</ref> While examining the reproductive behavior of ratites and tinamous, his study revealed a broad spectrum of mating systems, varying from monogamy to mixed polygyny/polyandry, underscoring their significant role in elucidating the adaptive implications of social structure, mating systems, and parental care strategies.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://academic.oup.com/biolinnean/article/25/1/77/2670707|title=The mating systems of ratites and tinamous: an evolutionary perspective – OUP|date=1985 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8312.1985.tb00387.x |last1=Handford |first1=Paul |last2=Mares |first2=Michael A. |journal=Biological Journal of the Linnean Society |volume=25 |pages=77–104 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> His investigation into the role of granitic outcrops as a selective force in mammalian evolution established the crucial role of granite outcrops around the globe in enhancing biodiversity in areas that are typically depauperate due to their semiarid or arid nature. He has conducted field research in the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica, Venezuela, Colombia, Brazil, Argentina, Egypt, Iran, and India.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://rswa.org.au/publications/Journal/80(3)/80(3)mares.pdf|title=The geobiological interface: Granitic outcrops as a selective force in mammalian evolution – RSWA}}</ref> Concentrating his research efforts on the unique adaptations and ecological characteristics of ''Tympanoctomys barrerae'', his study shed light on its poorly known natural history and provided evidence for its convergence with other desert-dwelling rodents with similar dietary and physiological traits.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/222492631|title=Evolutionary convergence of the highly adapted desert rodent Tympanoctomys barrerae – Researchgate}}</ref> His more recent work in 2017 focused on genetic diversity and taxonomy in the tribe Lasiurini, shedding light on the timing of hoary bat colonization in the Hawaiian Islands, and providing evidence for recognizing North American and Hawaiian hoary bats as distinct species.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Nuclear and mtDNA phylogenetic analyses clarify the evolutionary history of two species of native Hawaiian bats and the taxonomy of Lasiurini (Mammalia: Chiroptera)|first1=Amy B.|last1=Baird|first2=Janet K.|last2=Braun|first3=Mark D.|last3=Engstrom|first4=Ashlyn C.|last4=Holbert|first5=Maritza G.|last5=Huerta|first6=Burton K.|last6=Lim|first7=Michael A.|last7=Mares|first8=John C.|last8=Patton|first9=John W.|last9=Bickham|date=October 11, 2017|journal=PLOS ONE|volume=12|issue=10|article-number=e0186085|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0186085|pmid=29020097|pmc=5636129 |bibcode=2017PLoSO..1286085B |doi-access=free }}</ref>
